strengths: The paper addresses a timely and underexplored problem: test-time adaptation for vision-language object detectors rather than closed-set detectors or classification VLMs. The declared contribution type is Algorithms/General, and the work is appropriately assessed as a practical algorithmic framework plus benchmark.

The proposed components are well motivated for detection. IoU-weighted entropy uses proposal overlap structure to reduce the known failure mode of entropy minimization, and image-conditioned prompt selection addresses the weakness of naive prompt averaging for VLODs.

The experimental coverage is broad: two representative VLODs (YOLO-World and Grounding DINO), multiple domain shifts (style, driving, low-light, common corruptions), and extensive appendix results on PASCAL-C and COCO-C. The gains are consistent over zero-shot and several adapted TTA baselines.

The ablation studies are useful and go beyond a minimal evaluation, including adapter placement, prompt-generation strategies, hyperparameter sensitivity, top-M proposals, batch size, augmentation, larger backbones, and fine-tuning before adaptation.

The method is relatively lightweight and practical for TTA: it resets per image, adapts only small adapter/residual parameters, reports throughput and trainable parameter overhead, and avoids requiring target labels or source data.
weaknesses: The novelty is incremental in mechanism: the method combines entropy minimization, adapter tuning, prompt selection, and proposal clustering in a sensible way, but the individual ideas are fairly simple extensions of existing TTA/VLM practices. The main novelty is their adaptation to VLODs rather than a fundamentally new optimization principle.

Several gains are modest in important regimes. On Cityscapes and BDD100K, improvements over zero-shot are small, especially for YOLO-World, and the paper itself notes weakness on scenes with many tiny low-overlap objects. This limitation matters because driving scenes are a central motivation for robust detection.

The baseline comparison is broad but not fully conclusive. Existing OD-TTA methods that use pseudo-label filtering, teacher models, or stronger multi-step/augmentation pipelines are described as heavier, but not all are directly compared under matched compute. The appendix shows augmentations can produce very large gains, yet the main comparisons do not clearly establish whether VLOD-TTA plus/versus augmented baselines is the decisive factor.

Hyperparameter and design choices appear somewhat target- and architecture-dependent: different adapter locations for YOLO-World and Grounding DINO, different fusion coefficients, selected IoU thresholds/exponents, and top-M choices. The paper reports sensitivity curves, but it is not fully clear how these would be selected in a truly unlabeled deployment without tuning on benchmark performance.

Reproducibility is only partial. The abstract has an empty code placeholder, exact GPT prompt generation procedure is not fully specified beyond examples, and some implementation details of adapting baselines to object detection could be more explicit. No variance, confidence intervals, or multiple-run stability analysis is reported, which is relevant for per-image adaptation.

The prompt-selection score averages prompt compatibility over all proposals, which may be biased by background-dominated or noisy proposal sets. The paper shows empirical effectiveness, but the theoretical justification is weak and failure cases beyond small-object scenes are not deeply analyzed.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and timely problem: test-time adaptation for vision-language object detectors under domain shift, a setting that is less explored than classification TTA for VLMs.

The two proposed components, IoU-weighted entropy and image-conditioned prompt selection, are detection-specific and easy to understand. The use of proposal overlap is a plausible way to exploit structure already produced by detectors.

The experimental section covers several shift types, including stylized datasets, driving scenes, low-light images, and common corruptions, and evaluates both YOLO-World and Grounding DINO rather than only a single detector.

The paper includes useful ablations on adapter placement, prompt strategies, hyperparameters, batch size, augmentation, backbone scale, and fine-tuning before adaptation. The latency/parameter table is also helpful for assessing practical cost.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is fairly incremental. IoU-weighted entropy is a heuristic reweighting of standard entropy minimization by connected-component size, and image-conditioned prompt selection is a simple top-rho prompt filter based on mean proposal similarity. These are reasonable engineering ideas, but the paper does not provide a deeper analysis showing why they should reliably improve VLOD adaptation beyond the reported empirical trend.

The empirical gains are often modest, especially over the strongest Adapter baseline. For example, on Cityscapes and BDD100K the improvements for YOLO-World are small, and several reported advantages are around 0.3-1 mAP. This weakens the claim that the method is a broadly strong TTA framework rather than a tuned variant of adapter-based entropy adaptation.

The evaluation of baselines is not fully convincing. Several baselines are classification TTA methods adapted by the authors, but the paper gives limited detail on whether these adaptations were carefully tuned for detection. Strong object-detection TTA methods are discussed in related work but not substantively compared, even in adapted or partial form, so it is hard to know whether VLOD-TTA is competitive with the most relevant detection-TTA alternatives.

The method appears sensitive to implementation choices and dataset-specific tuning. Hyperparameters such as gamma, theta, rho, lambda, M, adapter placement, and prompt construction all matter, but the main results use fixed values that seem selected after extensive ablation. The paper does not clearly separate validation/tuning from test evaluation, which is especially important in a TTA setting with no labeled target data.

The prompt-generation setup raises reproducibility and fairness concerns. The main method uses GPT-generated prompt pools, but the exact generation protocol, model/version, randomness, and full prompt lists for all classes/datasets are not fully specified in the main paper. The abstract also has an empty 'Code:' field, so reproducibility is currently weak.

The appendix shows that adding a single scale augmentation gives very large AP50 gains on the style-shift datasets, much larger than some main-method gains, yet the main comparisons do not appear to include augmentation-enhanced versions of the baselines or of the full method. This makes the source of improvement and the practical best configuration unclear.

The proposed IoU-weighted objective can systematically disadvantage small or sparse objects because it rewards large proposal clusters. The paper acknowledges this for Cityscapes, but the limitation is central to detection and not adequately mitigated. A large false-positive cluster could also be reinforced by the same mechanism.

The IPS score is the mean prompt similarity over all proposals, which can be dominated by background proposals, frequent classes, or detector proposal biases. The paper does not sufficiently analyze failure cases or whether IPS selects semantically meaningful prompts across diverse scenes.

The claim of preserving zero-shot capability is not directly evaluated. Since the method resets per image, this is plausible, but the paper does not test whether adaptation harms performance on in-domain or mixed-domain streams, nor does it evaluate continual or streaming behavior beyond single-image adaptation.

The presentation is generally readable, but there are signs of incompleteness and polish issues, including the missing code link, occasional formatting problems, and some overstrong wording such as 'first' and 'significantly' relative to the modest gains and limited baseline evidence.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and timely gap: test-time adaptation for vision-language object detectors, rather than only closed-set detectors or vision-language classifiers. The framing is well motivated, and the claimed setting is relevant for robust open-vocabulary detection under realistic domain shift.

The method is technically sensible and detection-specific. IoU-weighted entropy uses the dense proposal structure of object detectors instead of treating proposals independently, and image-conditioned prompt selection tackles a real weakness of naive prompt averaging for VLODs.

The empirical evaluation is broad. The paper tests YOLO-World and Grounding DINO across stylized datasets, driving scenes, low-light images, and common corruptions, and includes multiple adapted TTA baselines. The gains are consistent across most settings, including both CNN-style and transformer-based VLODs.

The ablations are useful and fairly complete: prompt generation, adapter placement, IoU threshold, cluster exponent, prompt selection fraction, fusion coefficient, top-M proposals, batch size, augmentation, backbone scaling, and pre-adaptation fine-tuning are all examined.

The paper is generally clear, with intuitive figures explaining the failure mode of standard entropy minimization and the role of prompt selection. The qualitative examples support the proposed mechanism and help make the method easy to understand.

The contribution should be assessed as an Algorithms/General paper with a strong applied systems/benchmarking component. Under that framing, the combination of a simple method and a broad VLOD-TTA benchmark is valuable even though the individual ingredients are not radically new.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than high. Entropy minimization, adapters, prompt selection, and IoU/proposal consistency are all familiar ideas; the main contribution is their adaptation and integration for VLODs. This is useful, but the conceptual leap is limited.

The absolute gains are often modest, especially on Cityscapes and BDD100K, where improvements are around 1-2 AP. The method is most convincing on style shifts and corruptions, but less decisive in crowded scenes with many small objects, which the authors also acknowledge.

The baseline set is not fully satisfying. The paper adapts several VLM-classification TTA methods and includes an adapter entropy baseline, but it does not compare against stronger object-detection TTA methods adapted as carefully as possible to VLODs. This makes it harder to isolate whether the gains come from the proposed objective or from baseline mismatch.

The protocol raises some reproducibility and fairness questions. Hyperparameters such as gamma, rho, M, lambda, adapter placement, and prompt generation strategy appear selected from empirical behavior on target-style datasets; the paper should better specify any validation/tuning protocol compatible with true test-time adaptation.

The paper lacks statistical reliability analysis. Text-to-detection adaptation can be sensitive to optimizer settings, proposal filtering, prompt pools, and image order, but the results are reported without confidence intervals, repeated runs, or significance tests.

The evaluation of common corruptions is largely YOLO-World-only in the main and appendix tables. Since the method claims applicability across VLODs, broader corruption results for Grounding DINO would strengthen the empirical case.

The image-conditioned prompt score is a simple mean over proposals, which may be biased by background-heavy or numerous low-quality proposals. The paper motivates this empirically but could analyze failure cases more deeply, particularly when irrelevant prompts align with frequent background structures.

Some implementation details remain underspecified for reproducibility, including optimizer choices, learning rates, exact adapter insertion points in released configs, prompt generation procedure/model/version, random seeds, and whether code will be released; the abstract contains an unfinished 'Code :' field.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored problem: efficient test-time adaptation for vision-language object detectors, rather than only vision-language classifiers or closed-set detectors.

The proposed method is simple and detector-aware. IoU-weighted entropy uses proposal overlap structure in a sensible way, and image-conditioned prompt selection addresses a real weakness of uniform prompt averaging for detection.

The empirical evaluation is broad: two representative VLODs, multiple domain-shift datasets, common corruptions, larger backbones, specialized-domain evaluation, component ablations, hyperparameter sweeps, and runtime/memory comparisons.

Results are generally consistent. Gains over zero-shot and adapted TTA baselines appear across style shifts, low-light data, driving scenes, PASCAL-C, and COCO-C, with especially clear improvements over standard entropy/adapters on several datasets.
The paper is mostly clear and includes useful failure analysis, particularly for Cityscapes, where rider/person ambiguity and small objects expose limits of IoU-based clustering.
weaknesses: The algorithmic novelty is moderate. IWE is essentially entropy reweighting by predicted-class IoU component size, and IPS is a straightforward top-prompt selection by average image compatibility; the theoretical justification for IPS is mostly a simple cosine-Euclidean equivalence rather than a deeper guarantee.

Many improvements are modest over the strongest baselines. For example, the comparison to TTAOD-F on COCO-C is 26.2 vs. 26.0 mAP without warm-start, so the main advantage is efficiency rather than a large accuracy gain.

The method still has substantial test-time overhead relative to zero-shot inference: e.g., 20 FPS vs. 89 FPS for YOLO-World and 531.6 ms/img vs. 210.6 ms/img for Grounding DINO in the reported settings. The paper’s “low overhead” claim should be tempered accordingly.

Hyperparameter selection raises practical TTA concerns. The method uses several tuned values, including IoU threshold, cluster exponent, top-M proposals, prompt fraction, fusion coefficient, detector-specific adapter placement, and detector-specific lambda; it is not fully clear how these would be chosen without target labels in deployment.

IWE can reinforce wrong but spatially coherent predictions, especially for semantically overlapping labels or many small objects. The Cityscapes analysis shows person/rider AP degradation, which is a substantive limitation for open-vocabulary detection with fine-grained or overlapping categories.

Reproducibility is weakened by reliance on GPT-generated prompts, including “ChatGPT-5” in the manuscript, without a sufficiently complete prompt-generation/release protocol in the main paper. Baseline adaptation details also need enough precision to ensure fair reimplementation.

The paper does not report variance or statistical uncertainty, despite many small absolute gains, and some comparisons involve different operational settings such as TTAOD-F batch size/warm-start choices.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant and underexplored problem: test-time adaptation for vision-language object detectors under distribution shift. This is a meaningful computer vision setting, especially for open-vocabulary detectors deployed in changing environments.

The proposed method is simple and detector-aware: IoU-weighted entropy uses proposal overlap structure, while image-conditioned prompt selection addresses the known sensitivity of vision-language models to prompt wording.

The experimental section is broad in scope, covering YOLO-World and Grounding DINO across style shifts, driving datasets, low-light imagery, PASCAL-C/COCO-C corruptions, and several ablations. The paper also acknowledges an important failure mode on Cityscapes involving small objects and rider/person ambiguity.
The method usually improves over zero-shot and adapted TTA baselines, and the ablations suggest that both IWE and IPS contribute to the gains.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. IWE is essentially entropy minimization reweighted by connected-component size in an IoU graph, and IPS is top-k prompt filtering by average proposal-text similarity. These are reasonable engineering ideas, but the paper does not make a strong conceptual or theoretical advance beyond combining known TTA, adapter, proposal clustering, and prompt-selection ideas.

The experimental gains are often modest relative to the strongest baseline. On several main datasets, improvements over Adapter are small, and the comparison to the only specialized prior VLOD TTA method, TTAOD-F, is not very compelling by accuracy alone: default VLOD-TTA improves average COCO-C mAP only from 26.0 to 26.2, while still being much slower than zero-shot inference.

The claim of low overhead is overstated. The method requires backpropagation at test time and is reported at 531.6 ms/image versus 210.6 ms/image for zero-shot Grounding DINO on COCO-C; for YOLO-World, FPS drops from 89 to 20. This may be cheaper than TTAOD-F, but it is not obviously lightweight for practical real-time deployment.

The evaluation protocol raises reproducibility and fairness concerns. The manuscript leaves the code field blank, uses ChatGPT-5-generated prompts without providing complete prompt sets for all experiments, and appears to rely on several tuned hyperparameters. It is unclear how these hyperparameters were selected without target validation data, which is central to TTA.

The baseline comparisons are not fully satisfying. Several baselines are adapted from classification or cache-based VLM methods, and the strongest specialized prior method is only compared in limited settings. The TTAOD-F comparison also differs in batch size and initialization details, making the efficiency/accuracy trade-off hard to interpret cleanly.

The method has important structural limitations. Its core assumption that large overlapping proposal clusters are more reliable can fail for small objects, crowded scenes, and semantically ambiguous classes. The Cityscapes analysis shows that IWE can reinforce wrong class assignments, substantially reducing AP for person and rider before aggregation.

The IPS formulation is weakly justified. Averaging prompt compatibility over all proposals, including background and noisy proposals, is a crude image-level relevance signal. The supplementary 'theoretical justification' is only a cosine-Euclidean equivalence and does not establish that this score selects semantically appropriate prompts for detection.

Some experimental details are unclear or potentially inconsistent. The supplement reports very large gains from adding a single augmentation, but the main implementation description does not clearly state whether augmentation is used in the main results or how baselines are matched under that choice. This matters because TTA performance can be highly sensitive to such protocol choices.

The paper would benefit from statistical reporting, stronger analysis of sensitivity to prompt generation and random choices, and a clearer distinction between per-image reset adaptation and genuinely online deployment adaptation. As written, the evidence does not fully support the breadth of the claims.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and underexplored problem: test-time adaptation for vision-language object detectors under distribution shift. The motivation is convincing, especially the distinction from classification-oriented VLM TTA and from the heavier mean-teacher VLOD method TTAOD-F.

The proposed components are simple, well targeted to detection, and technically plausible. IoU-weighted entropy uses proposal overlap structure to reduce the influence of isolated boxes, while image-conditioned prompt selection tackles a real weakness of uniform prompt averaging for open-vocabulary detection.

The experimental coverage is strong for an Algorithms/General contribution: two representative VLODs, six shifted detection datasets, PASCAL-C/COCO-C corruptions, 15 corruption types, multiple metrics, and both CNN-style and transformer-style detector backbones. Gains are generally consistent rather than limited to one setting.

Ablations are useful and fairly extensive. The paper studies IWE vs. IPS, adapter vs. batch-norm updates, prompt averaging vs. selection, prompt-generation strategies, adapter placement, hyperparameter sensitivity, batch size, augmentation, fine-tuning before adaptation, larger backbones, and a specialized underwater domain.

The efficiency comparison is a meaningful part of the contribution. Compared with TTAOD-F on COCO-C, the method achieves comparable or better average mAP with far fewer total parameters and much lower memory, supporting the paper's claim of a better accuracy-efficiency tradeoff.

The paper is generally clear and well organized. The authors also discuss limitations such as small-object scenes, Cityscapes rider/person ambiguity, and remaining latency relative to zero-shot inference, which makes the empirical story more credible.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than high. The method combines entropy minimization, proposal clustering/IoU weighting, lightweight adapters, and prompt selection in a sensible way, but each ingredient is conceptually close to existing TTA, detection, and prompt-selection ideas. The main contribution is the effective adaptation of these ideas to VLODs rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic principle.

The efficiency claim needs careful framing. VLOD-TTA is much lighter than TTAOD-F, but it still requires backpropagation per test image and is substantially slower than zero-shot inference. For example, the reported GD COCO-C latency is 531.6 ms/img vs. 210.6 ms/img for zero-shot, and YOLO-World throughput drops from 89 FPS to 20 FPS. This is practical for some settings but not clearly real-time in all deployment scenarios.

The comparison to TTAOD-F is informative but not fully clean. The paper notes different batch-size behavior and uses a warm-start variant based on TTAOD-F initialization, but the main comparison still depends on implementation details that could affect both accuracy and memory. More standardized settings or additional reporting for batch size 1 vs. original settings would strengthen the case.

Reproducibility has some gaps. The manuscript has an empty 'Code:' field, and prompt generation relies on 'ChatGPT-5' with only a high-level instruction. Without released prompts, seeds, exact hyperparameters for all baselines, and implementation details for the adapted TPT/VPT/DPE baselines, reproducing the full benchmark may be difficult.

The method can reinforce coherent but wrong proposal clusters. The Cityscapes rider/person analysis demonstrates this risk: sharpening large overlap clusters may worsen fine-grained class ambiguity even when localization is correct. This limitation is acknowledged, but it is central to the proposed objective and may matter in safety-critical or long-tail open-vocabulary settings.

The gains on some realistic driving datasets are relatively small compared with the gains on style shifts and corruptions. This does not invalidate the contribution, but it narrows the strongest evidence to settings where proposal overlap is reliable and class ambiguity is limited.
